newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania reforms on track, need broader support-IMF.
newsitem.headline: Romania reforms on track, need broader support-IMF.

text.p: Romania's reforms have started to bear fruit and deserve broad international support, John Hill, the International Monetary Fund's representative in Bucharest, said on Wednesday.
"There are clear indications that the Romanian economy has begun to stabilise," Hill told a conference on investment opportunities, according to a text obtained by Reuters.
"We believe therefore that the government's programme deserves broad support, both at home and abroad."
The new centrist coalition government, which ousted ex-communists in last year's elections, launched a shock-therapy programme in February aimed at stepping up delayed reforms.
The programme won international lenders' support with the IMF approving a stand-by credit of $430 million followed last month by World Bank loans of more than $700 million.

Hill said a fall in monthly inflation to 4.3 percent in May suggested "the underlying rate of inflation is being brought under control". Central bank (BNR) foreign reserves were growing "at a faster pace than was envisaged".

Tough monetary policies and freeing of prices on staples and utilities had initially pushed monthly inflation to over 30 percent in March. Under government plans, it is to fall to two percent by the end of the year and the budget deficit is to be trimmed to 4.5 percent from last year's 5.8 percent.

The BNR's foreign exchange reserves soared to $1.49 billion at end-May from $697.4 million in February with the bank draining dollar excess from the market after growing foreign interest in Romanian capital markets.
Hill said an IMF mission would visit Bucharest in July to review progress.
"The discusion will focus on a revised budget for 1997," he said. "The government's plans to provide some tax relief will be evaluated in that context."
The review is expected to be formally concluded in September or October, when the Fund will set benckmarks for the second half of 1997, he added.
"Ultimately, the creation of new jobs and higher living standards...will depend to a large extent on a substantial increase in direct foreign investment," Hill said.
